subtitle: Center people who use services by developing decisions with them, not for them. You will learn to preserve their choices and show clearly how their knowledge changes the work.
scope: For leaders and supervisors developing policies, communications, or service processes in DSD and other DHS work areas. The course concerns participation in organizational decisions, not determination of an individual’s eligibility, capacity, benefits, or legal rights. Formal decisions remain with the people or areas responsible. Government-to-government matters defer to the person or area responsible within ADSA (Aging and Disability Services Administration). Course cases are practice; use de-identified learning notes and approved processes for real project records.
introTranscript: People with disabilities have knowledge of services that cannot be supplied only by administrative records or by professionals who support them. Centering that knowledge means more than placing a person on a committee. It involves an understandable decision, a genuine role, workable participation, and a response that shows what changed. This course builds on basic community-engagement planning. You will practice designing a partnership around a meeting invitation, navigating support-person roles, comparing service options, reviewing evidence, and following through when a project becomes difficult. The aim is a usable decision process, with choice and agency preserved. Participation in this learning is voluntary; required agency duties and approved procedures remain separate.

lessons.title: Work with people, rather than using them as examples
lessons.summary: A real partner can question the problem, develop options, and examine the result, rather than only supply a story.
lessons.objective: Distinguish participation as a contributor from participation limited to illustrating an agency message.
objectives: Distinguish participation as a contributor from participation limited to illustrating an agency message.
Define a decision role in which people with disabilities can influence problem framing or options.
Identify a recruitment assumption that could exclude a relevant perspective.
takeaways: A lived-experience story can inform work without being treated as permission to speak for the person.
Participants can contribute judgment, design ideas, and review, as well as personal accounts.
Disability does not imply one experience, preference, or position on a proposal.
lessons.statement: Invite people into the reasoning and choices, not only into the presentation.

image.caption: A meaningful role includes room to ask questions and shape the choices under discussion.

intro.heading: What role is actually being offered?
intro.body:
A leader may invite a person using services to open a meeting with their story and then continue the decision discussion without them. The story may be moving and relevant. Yet the person’s role is limited to illustrating the work of others. They cannot question the problem statement, propose an alternative, or examine the final recommendation. If the project is described as developed with people with disabilities, that limited role needs closer examination.

Centering people in organizational decisions means offering a role that can affect the work. For a new service-planning invitation, participants might identify what makes the current invitation confusing, help write questions, compare two drafts, and review whether the chosen version addresses the original difficulty. Staff can explain legal and administrative limits while preserving these opportunities. A meaningful role need not make a participant responsible for every technical detail or give them authority the agency cannot delegate.

Ask what contribution the team is prepared to receive. Does it want confirmation of an existing plan or examination of alternatives? Can a participant say the team is solving the wrong problem? Can they ask for a different response method or decline to share personal history? The way staff handle these choices often tells more about partnership than the number of seats on an advisory group.

People with disabilities have different experiences, cultures, resources, communication methods, and relationships to services. A person who uses one waiver service cannot represent everyone who uses another. Someone employed in a disability organization may contribute professional expertise alongside personal experience. Invite each person to define the perspective they are bringing. Do not ask them to carry an entire category, validate the agency’s intentions, or prove that their disability makes their opinion credible.

The Minnesota Olmstead Plan provides context for chosen community lives. This course applies that purpose to participation in decisions without claiming that every suggested partnership arrangement is a formal plan requirement. The practical question remains: what can people influence here, and how will the team make that influence visible?

inThisLesson: Examine what a participant role allows.
Keep personal storytelling voluntary.
Create space to question the problem.
Describe the limits of representation.
lessons.keyStatement: People can help develop the decision; they are not merely evidence for an agency story.

flashcards.back: Knowledge gained through one’s own experience. It can contribute to a decision without representing everyone with a similar identity.
A defined opportunity to help frame a problem, develop or review choices, and examine the response within clear authority.
A visible role with little opportunity to affect the work, such as being invited only to endorse or illustrate a settled decision.
The person’s ability to express preferences, make choices, question assumptions, and decide how they participate.
Someone the participant chooses or uses for assistance. The support role does not automatically authorize replacing the participant’s views.

items.title: Can the problem change?
items.body: A team may start with “people do not attend their planning meetings.” Participants may explain that the invitation arrives too late, uses unfamiliar wording, or does not make their own choices visible. Let that knowledge revise the problem statement. Treating the original explanation as fixed can lead to a solution that leaves the actual barrier untouched.

items.title: Can a participant disagree?
items.body: Explain how different opinions will be recorded and considered. A meaningful role permits criticism without requiring a personal story as justification. Leaders should demonstrate that disagreement will not determine access to services or the respect a person receives. Use the appropriate confidential route when a concern relates to the person’s own case.

items.title: Is the expected contribution clear?
items.body: Describe the task, time, information, and possible influence. Ask whether the person wants to review materials, discuss options, or contribute another way. Do not assume that everyone wants a leadership role or public visibility. Participation should not require accepting the agency’s preferred format simply to be included.

tabs.label: Experience
tabs.body: A person can describe how a process affected them, without disclosing everything about their services or diagnosis. Ask permission before using an identifiable account elsewhere.

tabs.label: Design
tabs.body: A participant can propose questions, compare alternatives, or identify an overlooked step. Their value is not limited to testimony about past difficulty.

tabs.label: Review
tabs.body: A participant can examine whether the revision addresses the original concern and whether the response represents their contribution accurately.

check.question: Which role offers a genuine partnership opportunity?
check.correct: Participants can question the problem, compare draft options, and review how their contributions affected the selected approach within clear decision limits.
wrong: One participant gives an inspiring story before staff privately choose the final approach.
The team invites a disability advocate only after the final draft is approved and asks for endorsement.
Staff select one participant to represent all disability experiences and approve every legal detail.
check.feedbackCorrect: The role includes influence across the reasoning and revision process without inventing authority or treating one person as everyone’s representative.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A visible story or endorsement can be valuable, but it does not establish shared development. Avoid both token roles and unrealistic expectations of representation or authority.

items.text: Participants help decide which questions the draft should answer.
A speaker provides a story but cannot join the option discussion.
One participant is expected to speak for all people with disabilities.
Participants review whether the revised instructions address the reported problem.
An invited guest appears only in the launch photograph.
A participant must disclose a diagnosis before offering design advice.

lessons.next: Next, prepare a partnership arrangement that respects people’s time and decision choices.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Leila sponsors a redesign of service-planning invitations. The project team plans to ask one person using services to tell a story at the launch meeting. Staff have already chosen a calendar-based digital invitation. Leila can reopen the invitation design and arrange a paid or unpaid participation approach only after the person or area responsible confirms the applicable arrangements.
scenario.prompt: What should Leila do to create a meaningful role?
options: Keep the story-only role because it avoids technical demands on the participant.
Explain the open design choices, invite several relevant experiences through approved channels, and offer roles in reviewing and testing alternatives.
Ask the invited speaker to certify that the digital invitation works for every person using services.
responses: This assumes the person cannot contribute to design and leaves the decision untouched. Offer choices instead of defining participation narrowly.
This turns participation into a practical opportunity while respecting different preferences and agency limits.
No participant can establish universal suitability from a single experience. The design needs broader evidence and specific testing.

lessons.transfer: Name one organizational decision in which participants could influence the problem, alternatives, or review. Which role currently offers only visibility?

move.control: You can change the participation role before recruitment and keep meaningful design choices open.
move.failure: A person appears in the presentation, but the team cannot identify any decision their contribution could change.
move.next: Write one partnership role statement and ask a colleague whether it describes actual influence rather than only attendance.

lessons.title: Agree on the role, preparation, and support
lessons.summary: A clear working agreement makes it easier to contribute without turning participation into unpaid, undefined responsibility.
lessons.objective: Draft a partnership arrangement covering purpose, influence, support, time, and follow-up.
objectives: Draft a partnership arrangement covering purpose, influence, support, time, and follow-up.
Identify one participation cost that should be considered before recruitment.
Explain how to discuss authorized compensation or reimbursement without making an unconfirmed promise.
takeaways: Preparation time and practical costs affect who can accept a role.
A participant should know what is requested and what they can decline.
Authorized payment arrangements, service questions, and benefit effects need the appropriate advice rather than assumptions.
lessons.statement: Respect for experience includes a workable task and an honest account of the conditions.

image.caption: A clear agreement reduces uncertainty about the task, the support, and what happens afterward.

intro.heading: Make the arrangement understandable
intro.body:
Participation can involve reading, travel, scheduling assistance, arranging care, and learning unfamiliar terms. A team may budget for staff time but assume participants can absorb these costs. That assumption changes who is able to contribute. Before recruitment, identify the requested work and the support the agency can provide. Keep the arrangement concrete: what will be reviewed, how long it may take, what sessions are expected, and whether written or other contributions are possible.

Explain influence separately from workload. A participant asked to read three drafts should know which parts can change and which role will consider their recommendations. If the team changes the scope or adds more work, discuss the change rather than treating the original agreement as open-ended. Participants can decline a session, a public quotation, or a personal question while still making a useful contribution within the agreed role.

Compensation and reimbursement deserve early attention, but do not invent rules or promise a payment that has not been authorized. Confirm applicable arrangements with the responsible agency staff. A person may have questions about the possible effect of payment on benefits or about travel reimbursement. Refer them to appropriate qualified assistance; neither the facilitator nor this course should decide the effect for an individual. Offer the information early enough to support an informed choice, and do not pressure someone to waive a payment or provide confidential financial information to the group.

Create an orientation that supports competence without implying people must become policy specialists. Explain the decision, key terms, options and timeline. Share materials in a usable form and ask what preparation method works. A participant may know the process intimately while being unfamiliar with agency acronyms. Staff may know the rule while overlooking what the process feels like. A partnership brings these kinds of knowledge together rather than treating one as sufficient.

Agree on feedback and exit. Explain how a participant can raise a concern about the arrangement, correct a summary, or stop participating. Explain the intended use of their contribution and the handling of identifying information. Do not promise absolute confidentiality for public or government records without checking applicable requirements. A careful agreement allows choice and participation without hiding limits.

inThisLesson: Identify the work and participation costs.
Explain influence separately from attendance.
Confirm practical and payment arrangements.
Offer a route for questions, changes, or withdrawal.
lessons.keyStatement: A participation agreement should describe what is offered and requested without requiring unnecessary disclosure.

items.title: The task and time
items.body: Describe the material, sessions, and expected preparation. Include a realistic estimate and ask whether the arrangement is workable. A participant should not discover at the first meeting that “a short review” means several evenings of reading. Revisit the plan if additional work becomes necessary.

items.title: Support and arrangements
items.body: Ask about communication, format, scheduling and other participation needs. Confirm what can be provided through the appropriate process. Explain any authorized reimbursement or compensation arrangement plainly, and give a contact for individual questions. Do not make assumptions about needs from a person’s diagnosis or appearance.

items.title: Use and choice
items.body: Explain whether contributions may appear in a public report and whether identification is optional. Ask before quoting a person, and use approved privacy and records practices. A participant can provide process knowledge without agreeing to be part of an agency campaign or to disclose their personal service history.

tabs.heading: Prepare both sides of the partnership

tabs.label: Participants
tabs.body: Offer a concise decision briefing, understandable questions, and a choice of preparation methods. Explain authority and how recommendations will be considered.

tabs.label: Staff
tabs.body: Prepare to hear unfamiliar priorities and to explain requirements without dismissing experience. Confirm who can change the draft and who can respond to access needs.

tabs.label: The facilitator
tabs.body: Keep the workload within the agreement, invite corrections, and give participants a way to raise concerns outside the group. Record role changes before continuing.

check.question: A participant asks whether an honorarium might affect their benefits. What is the appropriate response?
check.correct: Explain the confirmed payment arrangement and offer a route to qualified benefits advice, without making an individual eligibility determination or requesting private financial details in the group.
wrong: Promise that the payment can never affect any benefit.
Ask the participant to disclose all benefits and household finances during the meeting.
Require the participant to decline payment to avoid any possible question.
check.feedbackCorrect: The person receives usable information and a responsible advice route while their choice and privacy are preserved.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Avoid guarantees, compelled disclosure, or pressure to waive payment. A learning partnership does not authorize staff to decide an individual benefits question informally.

items.text: The expected reading and session time.
The team adds two more drafts to the review.
A question about an individual payment’s effect on benefits.
The intended use of participant comments in a report.
The project expands from a notice to a new service process.
A disputed formal accommodation determination.

lessons.next: Next, consider the relationship between a participant’s own voice and the assistance they choose.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Tomas invites participants to a “brief review” of a planning guide. A week later the team sends eighty pages and requests three evening meetings. One participant asks about travel reimbursement and benefit effects. Another wants to comment in writing. Staff worry that modifying the plan will create extra work.
options: Confirm support and any authorized payments, revise the workload and response choices, and route individual benefit questions to qualified assistance.
Keep the original request because people already agreed to participate.
Ask everyone to waive reimbursement and attend the same meetings to keep treatment identical.
responses: This repairs a changed arrangement and respects informed choice. It also gives the project a realistic basis for receiving useful input.
Agreement to a brief task is not agreement to unlimited new work. The project needs to revisit the conditions.
Identical conditions can produce unequal participation barriers. Do not treat a waiver of support as proof of fairness.

lessons.transfer: Draft five lines for one participation role: purpose, influence, workload, support, and use of input. Which arrangement still needs confirmation?

move.control: You can confirm the conditions before recruitment and renegotiate when the requested work changes.
move.failure: People are invited as partners but absorb undefined work and receive unverified answers about payment or service consequences.
move.next: Before recruiting one review group, confirm the participation arrangement with the responsible agency staff and provide a clear questions contact.

lessons.title: Keep the person’s voice present when support is involved
lessons.summary: Communication assistance and chosen supporters can strengthen participation without automatically replacing the person’s preferences.
lessons.objective: Identify a discussion practice that redirects a person’s voice to a supporter without checking their choice.
objectives: Identify a discussion practice that redirects a person’s voice to a supporter without checking their choice.
Develop a response that allows communication time and asks how the person wants assistance to work.
Distinguish support in a group decision discussion from a formal determination of legal authority.
takeaways: Address the person and ask how they want to contribute.
Allow communication supports and time without treating pace as evidence of ability.
Formal legal-authority questions belong to the responsible process, not a facilitator’s guess.
lessons.statement: Support should help the person participate in the way they choose, rather than quietly transfer their role to someone else.

image.caption: A listener can preserve a person’s contribution by allowing time and checking how assistance should work.

intro.heading: Whose view is being recorded?
intro.body:
In a meeting, staff may look toward a family member when the person using services pauses or uses a communication device. The family member may offer useful information and may be providing assistance the person wants. The problem arises when the team assumes that assistance means the supporter should answer every question or that their preferences are interchangeable. A person can need communication support and still have a view that differs from the supporter’s.

Start by addressing the participant. Ask how they want to contribute and what role their supporter should have. A person may prefer a supporter to help interpret a question, organize a response, or share background while the person answers. Another may want to submit a written response privately. The arrangement can change between tasks. Do not make the participant repeat a diagnosis to receive time or a usable format.

Keep different accounts separate. If a person says they want evening meeting options while a supporter prefers daytime, record both perspectives accurately. Explore the reasons without deciding that one automatically overrules the other. For an organizational design discussion, the task is to understand the implications for a service process. It is not an informal assessment of the person’s decision-making capacity or legal representation.

Formal authority may matter in specific service or legal decisions. When it does, use the authorized process and qualified staff rather than applying a general rule from this course. Do not assume that a relative is a legal representative, that a guardian’s authority covers every subject, or that the presence of any representative eliminates the need to hear the person. The course supports respectful participation; it does not interpret an individual court order.

Facilitation choices matter. Ask one question at a time, offer the question in advance when suitable, pause long enough for the selected communication method, and check the recorded meaning. Avoid rewarding the fastest response by moving the whole discussion around it. A supporter can be an important partner in making participation possible, and staff can preserve that contribution while keeping the person’s own perspective visible.

inThisLesson: Ask how assistance should work.
Allow time for different communication methods.
Record differing perspectives accurately.
Route formal authority questions without making assumptions.
lessons.keyStatement: Do not infer whose view should control from who answers fastest.

items.title: Ask before redirecting
items.body: If a participant is taking time to respond, do not automatically ask the supporter to answer instead. Offer a pause or another method and check what the person prefers. The person may welcome help, but that choice should not disappear because the agenda is crowded. A short break can be more respectful than interpreting silence as agreement.

items.title: Separate support from substitution
items.body: A supporter may help make a question understandable, recall details, or relay a response. Check whose words are being recorded and how the participant wants them used. If the supporter offers their own perspective, label it as that perspective rather than attributing it to the person using services.

items.title: Know the limit of the meeting
items.body: A design group cannot settle a disagreement about legal authority or an individual service determination. Use the person or area responsible if that issue becomes relevant. Continue gathering process feedback where appropriate without requiring the person to resolve a private legal matter publicly.

tabs.label: The participant pauses
tabs.body: Offer time, repeat or rephrase the question if requested, and check whether the person would prefer another method. Do not equate the pause with lack of understanding.

tabs.label: The supporter answers first
tabs.body: Thank them for the contribution and ask how the participant wants their own view included. Avoid blame while making the roles clearer.

tabs.label: Views differ
tabs.body: Record the perspectives separately and investigate what they reveal about the design. Do not turn the group into a contest over the person’s legal capacity.

check.question: A participant using a communication device has not finished responding, and a supporter offers a different answer. What should the facilitator do?
check.correct: Allow time, ask how the participant wants assistance to work, and distinguish the participant’s response from the supporter’s own view.
wrong: Record the supporter’s answer as the participant’s because it was faster.
Exclude the supporter entirely, even if the participant wants their assistance.
Decide during the meeting that the participant lacks capacity to contribute.
check.feedbackCorrect: This protects the person’s role and permits chosen support without confusing two perspectives.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Do not substitute speed for authority or remove chosen assistance automatically. The facilitator should make participation workable and route formal issues appropriately.

items.text: Ask the participant whether they want the supporter to help explain a question.
Treat every supporter comment as the participant’s preference.
A question about the scope of an individual court order.
Offer time for a communication device response.
Interpret a pause as agreement and close the discussion.
A dispute about authority for a specific service decision.

lessons.next: Next, use participants’ priorities to compare real options while keeping evidence and decision responsibilities clear.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Mei facilitates testing of a meeting invitation. Devon uses a communication device and brings a chosen supporter, Alex. Devon begins describing a preference for an evening option. Alex says daytime is easier for transportation. A staff member asks Mei to record daytime as Devon’s preference because the agenda is behind schedule. No individual service determination is being made.
options: Record daytime because Alex spoke more clearly.
Ask Alex to leave so Devon must respond alone.
Allow Devon to finish, ask how support should work, and record the transportation perspective separately from Devon’s preference.
responses: This changes the person’s view to match the faster response and hides the design trade-off.
Support can be chosen and helpful. Removing it without checking Devon’s wishes creates another barrier.
This preserves both relevant accounts and helps the team compare meeting options without making an unauthorized personal determination.

lessons.transfer: Describe a de-identified facilitation moment where a participant’s view could be replaced. Write the question that would clarify how assistance should work.

move.control: You can manage the pace, clarify roles, and check whose view is recorded.
move.failure: A support relationship becomes an assumption that the person’s own contribution is unnecessary.
move.next: Add a brief role-and-communication check to the start of one participant review session and practice allowing responses to finish.

lessons.title: Let participants’ priorities shape the alternatives
lessons.summary: Comparing options with people using services means examining trade-offs against priorities they helped identify.
lessons.objective: Translate a participant concern into a criterion for comparing options.
objectives: Translate a participant concern into a criterion for comparing options.
Compare two designs for different effects rather than choosing only the fastest administrative approach.
Identify evidence still needed before claiming one alternative improves access.
takeaways: A concern can change the criteria, not only the wording of a final recommendation.
Convenience for the agency and usability for the person are distinct considerations.
Testing an alternative should include the barrier it is meant to address.
lessons.statement: Keep participants involved while the alternatives are still different enough to matter.

image.caption: Comparing drafts makes priorities concrete and allows people to point to the step that does or does not work.

intro.heading: From concern to decision criterion
intro.body:
A participant says, “I cannot tell whether I have a choice about who attends the meeting.” The team could add a reassuring sentence without changing the invitation process. It could also use the concern as a comparison criterion: does each option make the person’s choices understandable before anyone is invited? The second approach lets participants’ knowledge shape how the options are judged, not simply how the chosen option is presented.

Develop a short set of criteria with participants. For a service-planning invitation, these might include recognizing the meeting purpose, understanding available choices, being able to respond through a usable method, and knowing where to ask a question. Explain any required content or administrative constraints. Avoid using a vague category such as “user friendly” without defining the action the person should be able to take.

Compare alternatives using realistic tasks. Ask a reader to find how to request a different time, how to suggest attendees, or how to ask for help. Do not test only whether they like the color or whether they can repeat a sentence. When a task fails, ask where the difficulty occurred. The participant is helping examine the design; the task is not a test of intelligence or an assessment of their disability.

Record different effects. One draft may work well for a person reading independently but require several steps for someone using telephone assistance. A new digital feature may save staff time while leaving the original account-access barrier unresolved. Preserve these differences and consider whether more than one path is needed. A small test can reveal problems and guide revisions without proving that the revised design works for everyone.

Move from criteria to a recommendation with reasons. Explain which concerns an option addresses, what it leaves unresolved, and what further testing is needed. The person or area responsible retains its decision role and formal duties. Participants can still challenge assumptions and help improve the next version. The team should be able to trace at least one criterion to a participant concern and one revision to the comparison. Without that trace, “we designed it together” may describe a meeting rather than a changed decision.

inThisLesson: Turn a concern into an observable criterion.
Compare alternatives using a real task.
Notice different effects across response methods.
Recommend an option with limits and a next test.
lessons.keyStatement: Test whether an option addresses the reported barrier, not whether participants can adapt to the option.

items.title: Define the task
items.body: Use a task close to the real process, such as finding a way to change the meeting time. Give only the assistance the actual design provides, while preserving any communication support the participant uses. If staff must explain every step verbally, record that reliance rather than claiming the written invitation works independently.

items.title: Check the criterion
items.body: A criterion should describe a result a person can experience or a step they can complete. “Recognizes that they can propose another meeting time” is clearer than “understands empowerment.” Ask whether the criterion matters to participants and whether it can be examined without requesting private service details.

items.title: Retain trade-offs
items.body: One option may improve readability but add a step to telephone responses. Record the effect and consider an adjustment. Do not erase a problem because the option is otherwise popular. A recommendation can favor an alternative while still identifying unresolved access needs and who will investigate them.

tabs.heading: Three lenses for the same draft

tabs.label: The person’s choice
tabs.body: Can the reader identify what they can decide or ask to change? Check that the invitation distinguishes an option from a requirement.

tabs.label: A usable path
tabs.body: Can the person respond through the offered method with their selected support? Identify where the design depends on an account, device, or staff explanation.

tabs.label: Administrative work
tabs.body: Can staff handle the response reliably and within actual responsibilities? Examine workload without treating efficiency as the only criterion.

check.question: Participants say they cannot find how to request a different meeting time. Which comparison task best examines that concern?
check.correct: Ask readers using the offered response methods to locate and use the time-change option in each draft, then revise the step where it breaks down.
wrong: Ask whether each draft looks professional and choose the most popular color.
Count the words and select the shorter draft without testing the task.
Tell readers where the answer is before asking whether they can find it.
check.feedbackCorrect: The task checks the actual barrier and compares usable paths. It evaluates the design rather than the reader’s ability.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Appearance, word count, or giving the answer in advance does not show whether the design supports the reported choice.

items.text: A reader can locate a time-change option without guessing.
Two participants needed a staff explanation to submit the phone response.
The draft is accessible to everyone because three readers liked it.
The invitation identifies who can ask a question before the meeting.
One response path requires an account the participant does not use.
The fastest option for staff is automatically the fairest option.

lessons.next: Next, review the evidence behind the recommendation and protect what participants have chosen to share.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Noor leads a review of meeting invitations. Draft A is shorter but puts the request-for-change instruction behind a portal login. Draft B provides a phone and written response option but needs slightly more staff handling. Participants identified the ability to change the meeting time as a central concern. The team has tested appearance, but not that task.
scenario.prompt: Which step should Noor request before a recommendation?
options: Choose Draft A because a shorter document always improves access.
Test the time-change task through the available methods, compare its effects and staff responsibilities, and revise the recommendation using those results.
Let participants pick a preferred design without explaining required content or response handling.
responses: Length alone does not answer the reported barrier, especially when a key step requires an unavailable account.
This respects the participant-defined priority and examines the actual choice without ignoring operational responsibilities.
Participants need enough information to compare choices. A preference vote without the relevant constraints and tasks does not establish a workable design.

lessons.transfer: Write one participant concern as a testable criterion. Design a task that examines it in two options without using personal case information.

move.control: You can keep alternatives open, include participant-defined criteria, and request a task-based comparison.
move.failure: The team invites comments on appearance after choosing a process that retains the original access barrier.
move.next: For one draft decision, compare two options against a participant-defined task and record both improvements and unresolved effects.

lessons.title: Use experience and other evidence without overstating either
lessons.summary: A supported recommendation keeps lived experience, administrative information, and uncertainty visible.
lessons.objective: Distinguish a participant account, a measured pattern, and an interpretation in a decision summary.
objectives: Distinguish a participant account, a measured pattern, and an interpretation in a decision summary.
Identify a privacy risk in quoting or combining engagement information.
Write a recommendation that states an evidence gap without treating missing information as reassurance.
takeaways: An account can identify a serious problem without establishing how common it is.
Averages can miss barriers, while stories alone cannot establish population rates.
Use only the identifying information needed for an authorized purpose.
lessons.statement: Respecting experience includes describing what it shows and what it cannot establish on its own.

image.caption: A careful evidence record separates findings, interpretation, and questions still requiring investigation.

intro.heading: Keep the evidence types distinct
intro.body:
A participant describes waiting several weeks for a returned call. The administrative report shows that most calls receive a response sooner. These pieces of information may both be accurate. The participant may have encountered a handoff not included in the report, or the report may measure the first response rather than a resolved question. The team should investigate the difference instead of choosing the evidence that makes the existing process look better.

Distinguish an account, a measured pattern, and an interpretation. An account describes an experience. A measured pattern depends on defined data, coverage, and the way the measure was calculated. An interpretation proposes what may explain the result. Keep the definitions visible. If participants were recruited through an established advisory group, do not use their comments to estimate what all people using a service prefer. If data excludes abandoned attempts, do not claim it proves the whole process is working.

Respect the value of each source. Experience can reveal a question staff had not asked, explain the consequence of a delay, and suggest a different outcome measure. Administrative information can show whether a pattern occurs across records and help examine changes over time. Neither requires participants to surrender their story for public use. A summary can describe a barrier without including a person’s name, exact location, or service history.

Check privacy when combining information. A quotation that seems anonymous may identify someone when paired with a county, rare service, or unusual timeline. Keep real project records in approved locations and use appropriate access controls. Follow the relevant privacy and data practices processes for analysis and reporting. In course reflection, use practice or de-identified examples. Do not promise that a public discussion is confidential or that every government record can be erased on request.

A supported recommendation explains what the team knows, what it suspects, and what it will examine next. It might say: “Participants reported difficulty after a call was transferred. Current measures do not cover that handoff. We recommend testing a clearer contact route and reviewing resolution time.” That conclusion respects the experience, uses the data accurately, and does not treat the missing measure as evidence that no problem exists.

inThisLesson: Separate accounts, measurements, and interpretations.
Check what the administrative measure covers.
Protect identity in combined reports.
State a recommendation with its uncertainty and next inquiry.
lessons.keyStatement: Missing evidence is a question to investigate, not evidence that a barrier does not exist.

items.title: Check the claim
items.body: Ask what each source actually establishes. A person’s experience can support a process concern without proving a statewide rate. A response-time average can describe included calls without covering unresolved referrals. Rewrite claims that travel farther than their evidence. Record the limitation beside the recommendation rather than in an unrelated footnote.

items.title: Check the identity risk
items.body: Look at the combined details, not just the absence of a name. An unusual service and a small location can identify a participant. Use the minimum information needed for the authorized analysis and apply the responsible privacy process. Ask before using an identifying quotation, while recognizing that permission alone does not replace agency data requirements.

items.title: Check the next inquiry
items.body: Name what would help answer the unresolved question and who can examine it lawfully. The next step may be reviewing a defined measure, testing a draft, or seeking another perspective through approved channels. Do not request private records simply because more detail could make a report interesting.

tabs.label: What was heard
tabs.body: Describe the participant account accurately and explain the recruitment scope. Protect unnecessary identifying details.

tabs.label: What was measured
tabs.body: State the measure, included cases, time period, and exclusions where relevant. Avoid treating an average as every person’s experience.

tabs.label: What is recommended
tabs.body: Connect the proposed action to the concern and evidence. Identify what remains uncertain and what review will follow.

check.question: A report shows prompt first responses, while participants describe unresolved questions after transfers. Which conclusion is strongest?
check.correct: The first-response measure does not answer the transfer-resolution concern; examine the handoff and test an improvement before concluding that the whole process works well.
wrong: The participant accounts must be wrong because the average is favorable.
The participant accounts prove every transfer fails across the state.
No new measure exists, so there is no evidence of any barrier.
check.feedbackCorrect: This keeps both evidence sources intact and asks the question the current measure cannot answer.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Do not dismiss experience, generalize beyond the information, or treat missing data as reassurance. Examine the difference between the measured step and the reported problem.

items.text: A participant describes three transfers before receiving an answer.
The defined call log shows first-response time for included calls.
The handoff may be causing unresolved questions.
A person describes needing a supporter to use the response form.
A task test records which draft readers could use without staff explanation.
The new instructions may reduce repeated contacts.

lessons.next: Next, carry the partnership through the selected decision, review, and return response.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Camila prepares a recommendation on a contact process. Three participants describe unresolved calls after transfers. The team has a favorable average for the first answer but no measure of resolution. An early report includes a quote with a rare service and a small county, making one person recognizable. Camila can revise the report and request an approved handoff review.
options: Remove the accounts because they conflict with the average.
Publish the identifying quotation because it makes the report persuasive.
Protect the unnecessary identifying details, distinguish the two measures, and recommend a defined handoff review linked to the reported barrier.
responses: The data and accounts may describe different steps. Deleting the accounts loses the question that needs examination.
Persuasiveness does not justify exposing a participant. Use authorized reporting practices and a de-identified description where suitable.
This strengthens the recommendation by correcting both the evidence claim and the privacy risk.

lessons.transfer: Write a short finding with three sentences: what was heard, what current evidence shows, and what remains uncertain. Remove details that are not needed for the learning task.

move.control: You can require an evidence distinction and privacy review before the findings are shared.
move.failure: An average dismisses the reported barrier, or an engaging story is used without regard to identity and evidence limits.
move.next: Review one recommendation for evidence scope and unnecessary identifying details, then assign an approved inquiry to the most consequential gap.

lessons.title: Sustain the partnership through a difficult decision
lessons.summary: A credible partnership continues through constraints, disagreement, implementation, and review of the result.
lessons.objective: Prepare a response showing how participant priorities affected a decision and which concerns remain unresolved.
objectives: Prepare a response showing how participant priorities affected a decision and which concerns remain unresolved.
Identify a project change that requires revisiting the participation agreement.
Choose a follow-up check that examines the effect on people using the process.
takeaways: A partnership is tested when the agency cannot accept every suggestion.
Participants should hear what changed and why, without being asked to endorse the entire result.
The review should examine whether the change helped, not just whether it launched.
lessons.statement: Keep the person’s role visible after the decision becomes harder, not only when the discussion is encouraging.

image.caption: Follow-through includes explaining the selected option and checking its effect with the people it is meant to help.

intro.heading: Return the decision and review its effect
intro.body:
Projects change. A budget adjustment may narrow an option. A required form may need to remain. A decision-maker may select an alternative that participants did not prefer. These moments can reveal whether the partnership was a genuine opportunity or a promise intended only to produce a favorable launch message. Leaders should return a specific account of the decision and its reasons while preserving the concerns people raised.

Describe the underlying priority, the chosen response, and the remaining issue. If participants wanted control over meeting times and the agency retains a scheduling limit, explain the confirmed limit and what alternatives remain. Do not say “we could not do it” when part of the process can still change. Do not ask participants to endorse the full proposal as proof that they were heard. A person can recognize that their contribution mattered and still disagree with the final choice.

Revisit the arrangement when the project changes materially. A group that reviewed invitation wording has not necessarily evaluated a new portal requirement. Explain the change, the open choices, and the additional work requested. Give participants the opportunity to accept a revised role or decline. If a deadline prevents another review, describe the limitation honestly and plan an appropriate later check rather than claiming that previous participation covered the new issue.

Connect implementation to the original concern. A launch date establishes that a change occurred, not that it improved people’s experience. Ask whether readers can find and use the time-change option, whether telephone responses are handled reliably, and whether the person’s chosen support remains possible. Use approved data and engagement practices, and record uncertainties. If the barrier remains, revise the process rather than blaming participants for not using it correctly.

Staff can carry this work with guidance from the consultant. They should develop the recommendation, return the response, and examine the result within their responsibilities. The consultant can offer leadership, knowledge, and feedback without becoming the person who does every project task. A finished partnership record should let a colleague see the role offered, the influence exercised, the reasons for the decision, and the next review. That record gives the next project a stronger starting point.

inThisLesson: Explain a difficult decision respectfully.
Revisit a changed participation role.
Check the original barrier after implementation.
Carry responsibility with optional consultant guidance.
lessons.keyStatement: The response should preserve both the participant’s contribution and the fact that they may still disagree.

accordion.heading: Follow-through when the choice is difficult

items.title: A suggestion cannot be adopted
items.body: Explain the verified reason and consider another way to address the underlying concern. Distinguish a legal requirement from a staff preference or an assumption about workload. Offer a clear route for an issue held by another office. Do not imply that a respectful response requires the participant to agree.

items.title: The scope changes
items.body: Tell participants what changed and why. Explain the new task and decision opportunity before using their earlier contribution to support it. If further participation is requested, confirm access and practical arrangements again. Previous agreement to one task is not permission for any future use of the person’s account.

items.title: The result falls short
items.body: Return to the concern and examine where the revised process failed. Review the design, the implementation, and the evidence. Ask participants through appropriate channels whether the change addressed the difficulty. A candid correction is more useful than describing a launch as success while unresolved barriers remain.

tabs.heading: A partnership record people can recognize

tabs.label: What influenced the work
tabs.body: Name a participant-defined priority, criterion, or revision. Avoid substituting the number of meetings for evidence of influence.

tabs.label: What the agency decided
tabs.body: State the choice, confirmed reasons, and remaining questions. Do not describe disagreement as failure to understand the project.

tabs.label: What happens next
tabs.body: Assign the review, explain how participants can correct the account, and keep future commitments realistic. Use the people or areas responsible for formal matters.

check.question: Participants reviewed invitation wording, but the final proposal adds a required portal account. What should the leader do?
check.correct: Treat the portal requirement as a material change, explain it and its limits, and arrange an appropriate review or clearly report the gap rather than claiming prior participation covered it.
wrong: State that participants approved the complete process because they reviewed the wording.
Ask participants to endorse the new requirement so the report can describe agreement.
Use the earlier meeting photograph as evidence that the new account step was accessible.
check.feedbackCorrect: The leader keeps the participation claim tied to the actual scope and creates a defensible next opportunity.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Prior participation does not automatically cover a new process requirement. Endorsements and photographs cannot substitute for examining the added barrier.

items.text: Explain why required notice content remains and what was changed around it.
Confirm new work and access arrangements when the project expands.
Test whether readers can use the selected time-change method after launch.
Describe an unresolved concern and the office responsible for its next step.
Ask whether participants want to continue in the changed role.
Examine whether telephone responses are completed reliably.

lessons.next: Use the job aid to develop or review one partnership arrangement. Keep the decision, the person’s role, and the effect of the work connected.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Anika’s team revises planning invitations with participants who use services. Their priorities included changing meeting times without a portal account. A later technology decision adds that account step to reduce staff handling. The launch report says the full process was designed with participants. Anika can challenge the claim, request an alternative-path review, and arrange a response from the responsible manager.
scenario.prompt: Which course of action best sustains the partnership?
options: Correct the scope claim, explain the changed decision, examine an alternative response path, and return a response with a result-review plan.
Keep the launch language because correcting it may make the project look unsuccessful.
Ask participants to do all follow-up work because they requested the change.
responses: This preserves truthful participation and connects the unresolved concern to a practical next decision and review.
Avoiding embarrassment is not a reason to attribute an unreviewed choice to participants. Correcting the record protects the relationship.
Participants can contribute, but the agency remains responsible for its process and follow-through. Do not transfer that obligation to them.

lessons.transfer: Prepare a de-identified partnership record for one decision: offered role, participant priority, influence, decision reason, unresolved issue, and next review. Which entry is hardest to substantiate?

move.control: You can keep claims accurate, revisit changed roles, and require a review of the effect after launch.
move.failure: The agency reports shared design for unreviewed choices and treats implementation as proof that the original barrier was resolved.
move.next: At the next decision review, return a clear account of participant influence and agree on one check of the result with the responsible manager.

jobAid.subtitle: Keep choice, influence, evidence, and follow-through visible.
remember: Ask people how they want to contribute and use support.
A visible seat is not proof of influence.
Keep formal decisions, private information, and agency responsibilities in their proper processes.

sections.heading: Offer a real role
items: State the decision and what can change.
Offer influence over the problem, criteria, alternatives or review where authority permits.
Avoid asking one participant to represent every disability experience.
Keep personal storytelling and public identification optional within the approved arrangement.

sections.heading: Confirm the arrangement
items: Explain preparation, sessions, time and how input will be used.
Ask about communication and other participation needs.
Confirm authorized support, reimbursement or compensation arrangements.
Route individual benefits and formal authority questions to qualified assistance.

sections.heading: Preserve the person’s voice
items: Address the participant and ask how chosen support should work.
Allow time and alternative response methods.
Record a supporter’s own perspective separately when it differs.
Do not infer capacity or legal authority from appearance, speech, diagnosis or meeting pace.

sections.heading: Compare and support the recommendation
items: Translate a participant concern into a clear comparison criterion.
Test alternatives using a relevant task.
Separate accounts, measures and interpretations.
State evidence gaps and protect identifying details.
Use the required agency equity-analysis process; this course exercise is not a substitute.

sections.heading: Return and review
items: Explain what changed, what did not, and the confirmed reasons.
Revisit materially changed tasks or participation promises.
Do not require participants to endorse the complete decision.
Review whether the original barrier improved and assign remaining actions.
Ask the consultant for guidance and feedback while staff carry out their work.
